newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African markets warm to Manuel's first budget.
newsitem.headline: S.African markets warm to Manuel's first budget.

text.p: South Africa's markets gave a warm reception to Finance Minister Trevor Manuel's maiden budget on Wednesday, in particular his moves to widen exchange control relaxation to include individuals for the first time.
The rand rallied around two cents against the dollar following the news, long bonds yields dipped as Manuel started speaking and stocks advanced.
The big budget numbers, including the four percent deficit target for 1997/98, were largely in line with expectations, though real spending was cut further than many had forecast.
Herman van Papendorp, economist at SMK Securities in Johannesburg, said the targeted increase in spending of just 6.1 percent -- 2.4 percent below expected inflation -- could prove hard to achieve.
But the move to relax exchange controls was seen as a significant advance, holding out the prospect of a widespread shift in capital controls.
The details of how much individuals will be able to take offshore or hold in foreign currency accounts from July 1 will only be given out later.
Reserve Bank governor Chris Stals told reporters in a pre-budget briefing that South Africa was now clearly in the second half of a continuing process to dismantle exchange controls.
Investors say removing exchange controls is important to demonstrate the government's own confidence in its policy.

Constantin Vayenas, emerging market economist at UBS in London, said the latest moves would reinforce economic policy discipline since individual South Africans would in future vote with their wallets by selling rand if the government veered off course.
"I think the moves on exchange controls are long overdue, but very positive. It is what everyone has been looking for," said Henry Flint, economist at stockbroker Mathison and Hollidge.
"I think from now on we can expect exchange controls to be removed more rapidly."

Dave Sadler of First National Bank in Johannesburg said the budget overall looked investor-friendly, delivering on the promised deficit reduction, easing exchange controls and cutting the marketable securities tax on share transactions.
But some analysts expressed disappointment that Manuel had not opted to change the tax on retirement funds from one based on income to one based on a fund's total assets.
